## Rome on a timeline

::: {.timeline}
- **753 BC** · Legend says Romulus founds the city of Rome.
- **509 BC** · Romans remove their last king. Rome becomes a {{< vocab "republic" >}}.
- **44 BC** · Julius Caesar is killed.
- **27 BC** · Augustus becomes the first {{< vocab "emperor" >}}. The {{< vocab "empire" >}} begins.
- **AD 80** · The {{< vocab "Colosseum" >}} is finished.
- **AD 476** · The western half of the empire falls.
:::

::: {.small-note}
AD years count *up* from year 1: AD 80 came before AD 476.
:::

## A city on seven hills

- The legend: twin brothers **Romulus and Remus** were raised by a wolf. Romulus founded Rome and named it after himself.
- What historians think: villages on seven hills slowly joined into one city.
- Rome was near the middle of Italy, close to the sea, on the River Tiber: good for farming and trade.

::: notes
The wolf story is a myth, like the Greek myths in Unit 1. Ask: why would a city want an exciting founding story?
:::

## The Republic: no more kings

```{python}
#| output: asis
print(card_grid(pick(terms, "republic", "senate", "consul"), zh=True))
```

::: notes
Two consuls, chosen for one year, could each block the other. Romans had had a bad king and never wanted one person to hold all the power again.
:::

## Athens and Rome: who decides?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.callout-note title="Athens: democracy 民主" icon=false}
Citizens vote on the **laws themselves**, in the Assembly.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.callout-tip title="Rome: republic 共和国" icon=false}
Citizens **elect leaders** ({{< vocab "consul" text="consuls" >}}), who make decisions with the {{< vocab "senate" >}}.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.small-note}
Many countries today are republics: people elect leaders to decide for them.
:::

## Julius Caesar

- A famous general who won wars in Gaul (today's France).
- He took control of Rome and made himself dictator for life.
- In **44 BC**, a group of senators killed him. They wanted to save the {{< vocab "republic" >}}…
- …but after years of civil war, Rome got an {{< vocab "emperor" >}} anyway.

## Augustus and the empire

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- Caesar's adopted son Octavian won the civil war.
- In **27 BC** he took the name **Augustus** and became the first {{< vocab "emperor" >}}.
- About 200 years of peace followed across the {{< vocab "empire" >}}: the *Pax Romana*, "Roman peace".
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](images/augustus-prima-porta.jpg){.photo .tall fig-alt="A marble statue of Augustus in armor, one arm raised"}

[A marble statue of Augustus, about 2,000 years old.]{.photo-caption}
:::
::::

## The Roman army

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- A {{< vocab "legion" >}} had about 5,000 soldiers, all Roman citizens.
- Soldiers marched with heavy packs and built a camp every night.
- They also built roads, bridges and walls across the {{< vocab "empire" >}}.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/trajans-column-legion.jpg){.photo fig-alt="A stone carving of Roman soldiers with shields, from Trajan's Column"}

[Roman soldiers carved on Trajan's Column in Rome, about AD 113.]{.photo-caption}
:::
::::

::: notes
The roads the army built are part of the next deck: Roman engineering.
:::
